ploughman.description: A person who tills the land with a plough, usually drawn by bullocks.

greens.description: Leafy vegetables, a common part of rural Odia cuisine.

Dharama.description: Dharama is a poor farmer who suffers abuse from the local Brahmin and struggles with the burdens of land and family responsibilities. He is often at the center of the village's disputes and hardships.

Barajua.description: Barajua is a familiar or affectionate form of address for Baraju, used by other characters, especially Dharama.

Dharama Baura.description: Dharama Baura refers to Dharama himself, with 'Baura' being an honorific or descriptive suffix.

Dharma Bou.description: Dharma Bou is Dharama's wife, mentioned in the context of keeping the household keys safe.

Mangala Thakuguni.description: Mangala Thakuguni is a woman whose hut serves as a gathering place for villagers in the evening.

Jal Khatei.description: Jal Khatei is a villager who sits in the circle during the evening gathering.

Jad Subhara.description: Jad Subhara is another villager present at the evening meeting.

Rup Jena.description: Rup Jena is a villager who participates in the group discussions.

Bhoti Goshthi.description: Bhoti Goshthi is a villager present at the gathering.

Ag Mundia.description: Ag Mundia is a woman who sits quietly near Mangala during the meeting.

Malati.description: Malati is a woman present at the evening gathering.

Rupa.description: Rupa is a villager, possibly a woman, who reflects on the hardships and fate of the villagers.

Uda.description: Uda is the village carpenter who comments on the lack of unity among the villagers.

Apat.description: Apat is a villager mentioned as an example of someone who has suffered misfortune.

Dhadukh.description: Dhadukh is another villager cited as an example of shared suffering.

Dama.description: Dama is a villager whose house has been burnt, symbolizing communal suffering.

Guruch.description: Guruch is a villager mentioned in Baraju's speech, possibly as a symbol of resilience.

Amar.description: Amar is a villager whose absence is lamented as a loss to the community.

Old Ratana.description: Old Ratana is an elderly villager who acknowledges the collective suffering of the group.

Jadu Dalai.description: Jadu Dalai is a villager who comments on the importance of unity and the futility of discord.

Rupaguai.description: Rupaguai is a villager addressed in a discussion about family quarrels and unity.

Baralu.description: Baralu is a villager who advocates for reconciliation and harmony.

Jahu.description: Jahu is a villager who joins the group at the end of the chapter.

Nathu.description: Nathu is a villager who joins the group at the end.

Roopa.description: Roopa is a villager who joins the group at the end.

Nebhara.description: Nebhara is a villager who joins the group at the end.

Dhenā.description: Dhenā is an old villager who reflects on the transience of life.

Jadu Dalera.description: Jadu Dalera is a villager who philosophically comments on the way of the world.

Mishra Brahmin.description: Mishra Brahmin refers to a member of the Mishra caste, a Brahmin family in the village, often associated with landownership and authority.

Baighara.description: Baighara is a type of hut or shelter, possibly used by cattle herders or as a temporary dwelling.

Gramchandra.description: Gramchandra refers to an auspicious or inauspicious star or astrological influence believed to affect one's fate.

Sravan Gramchandra.description: Sravan Gramchandra refers to a specific astrological star or period considered unlucky in local belief.

Gandhya.description: Gandhya is the name of a clan or family group in the village.

Meru.description: Meru refers to Mount Meru, a sacred mountain in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist cosmology, symbolizing something immense or unyielding.

landlords.description: Large landowners who lease land to tenant farmers or laborers.

handman.description: Likely a local term for an enforcer or henchman, possibly working for landlords or moneylenders.

Gubha.description: A local ritual or recitation performed for unity or protection, specific to Odia rural culture.

cartloads.description: A measure of quantity, referring to the amount that can be carried in a cart, often used for straw or grain.

rice gruel.description: A simple, watery porridge made from rice, commonly eaten by the poor in rural India.

Bancha.description: A villager who interacts with Baraju and Rupa, sometimes providing comic relief or commentary.

Sana.description: A member of the household or village, Sana is depicted as simple and sometimes bewildered by events.

Bhaba.description: A figure whose actions are referenced as a model for others, likely an elder or respected person in the community.

Sanath.description: A member of the household, Sanath is involved in discussions about family matters and expresses uncertainty about the future.

Muruka.description: A villager who makes lighthearted comments about family events.

Sao.description: A villager involved in discussions about land and harvest with Baraju.

Sarat.description: A villager who questions Baraju about the division of crops.

Sanabohu.description: A female member of the household, possibly a daughter-in-law, referenced in relation to a sari.

Bhamana.description: A villager or family member who is confused about household matters.

Harimise.description: A villager who comments on family disputes and traditions.

Mishra Akhimika Maai.description: An elder woman, possibly a respected matriarch or wise figure in the village.

Neus Ohba.description: A villager who criticizes others' actions and sense of responsibility.

Manjira Manisha Sanath.description: A villager who defends Baraju's actions and contributions to the household.

Chandar.description: A villager expected to speak at a gathering.

Jagua.description: A villager expected to speak at a gathering.

Baraku Pradhan.description: A variant of Baraju's name, possibly used to emphasize his stature or as a term of respect.

Baju Pradhan.description: Another variant of Baraju's name, used in the context of his fearlessness.

Regi.description: A villager or symbolic figure representing the suffering poor.

Daramal.description: A villager or symbolic figure representing the suffering poor.

Madua.description: A villager or symbolic figure representing the suffering poor.

Dharama Bauro.description: A figure invoked in prayer, possibly a deity or personification of dharma (righteousness).

Nabhei Maharana.description: A villager in distress, seeking help from Baraju for his sick child.

Nabha Maharana.description: Another spelling of Nabhei Maharana, described as a poor and struggling villager.

Barunei.description: A person referenced as Baraju's parent, indicating lineage.

Amin.description: A government land surveyor or revenue official.

Baisakh.description: The first month of the Odia (and Hindu) calendar, typically April-May, associated with harvest and new beginnings.

Sunar.description: A person or family in the village, possibly of the goldsmith caste.

Aj Bhenika.description: A villager, possibly an elder or respected figure, referenced for his wisdom.

Chak Muga.description: A specific plot or field in the village, associated with muga (a type of crop or land).

Dekhura’s Chandan.description: A reference to a person named Dekhura and his sandalwood stick, possibly symbolic or literal.

Koda Rishi.description: A sage or wise figure from local folklore, invoked for comic effect.

ru ta kansara gharara paagu.description: An Odia proverb or saying, likely referencing household wisdom or tradition.

am shoikshaghara.description: A specific household or storage place, possibly a granary or family room.

Satya, Dwapara, Kali.description: The three ages (yugas) in Hindu cosmology: Satya Yuga (age of truth), Dwapara Yuga, and Kali Yuga (current age of darkness).

Maharana.description: A caste or occupational title, often referring to carpenters or artisans in Odisha.

plough cattle.description: Oxen or bullocks used for ploughing fields in traditional agriculture.

manias.description: A traditional unit of land measurement or quantity, specific to the region.

chhakidas.description: Members of a family or group who have separated their share, possibly referring to divided households.

IOU.description: A written acknowledgment of debt, used informally to borrow money.

paisa.description: A subunit of Indian currency, 1/100 of a rupee.

bohu.description: Daughter-in-law in Odia and other Indian languages.

shopkeeper’s house.description: A household in the village associated with running a shop, often a distinct social or economic unit.

wedding house.description: A household where a wedding is taking place, often the center of social activity during the event.

central house.description: The main or ancestral house in a joint family, where important decisions and gatherings occur.

Baraju Padhaan.description: A key male character, responsible for household rituals and property matters; often seen as the head of the family.

Maipi.description: A woman frequently involved in household affairs, particularly in arranging chores and weddings.

Rghara.description: Mentioned as the father of Rula; likely a villager or family relation.

Rula.description: Son of Rghara, mentioned in the context of village families.

Swaghara.description: Mentioned as the father of Ghu; another villager or family relation.

Ghu.description: Son of Swaghara, part of the extended village community.

Kulura.description: Referenced as an object of devotion; possibly a deity or spiritual figure.

Naim.description: A character involved in the discussion about separating cooking pots; possibly a family member.

Bajku.description: A person writing near the house; possibly another name or nickname for Baraju.

Baraja.description: Another spelling for Baraju, involved in family leadership and property matters.

Dharu.description: A person who takes care of the chhakadi and has learned from Hari Mishra.

Ghoshei.description: Mentioned in relation to Dharu; possibly another villager or family member.

Hagu.description: A family member whose wedding expenses are discussed.

Bhone.description: Addressed by Baraju, possibly a term for a younger brother or close male relative.

Palanka.description: Mentioned as someone to be taken to the house near the school; likely a family member.

Haghabou.description: A variant spelling of Hagaboja, involved in the discussion about leaving the home.

Kauka.description: A character who feels uneasy about abandoning the home.

Bidagun.description: Mentioned in reference to another family that left their home; likely a villager.

Kanchika.description: A month in the Odia calendar, marking a specific time in the agricultural cycle.

karmabandhua.description: A term referring to a person bound by duty or karma, often used to describe a devoted spouse.

kansa.description: Bell metal, a traditional alloy used for making utensils in Odisha.

gulpa.description: A type of tree, often used as a landmark in Odia villages.

mung beans.description: A type of small, green legume commonly used in Indian cooking.

deer skin.description: Animal hide used in traditional rituals and ceremonies.

almanac.description: A traditional calendar or book of auspicious dates, used for planning rituals.

main rope.description: The primary rope used for drawing water from a well, essential in daily rural life.

verandah.description: A roofed platform along the outside of a house, common in Indian homes.

Haraboad.description: A male family member suffering from fever, involved in the household's packing and property matters.

Hagbou.description: A quiet family member who does not voice opinions about the family's decisions.

Shaighaboi.description: One of the village women who gathers at the headman's house to discuss the family's situation.

Padma.description: A villager who gathers with others to discuss Baraju's decision.

Nadhu.description: A villager, often emotional, who discusses the family's fate and expresses concern about Baraju's departure.

Dharma.description: A villager who worries about the consequences of Baraju leaving and the future of the household.

Maga.description: A villager who questions the value of staying in the village and discusses the leadership of the Pradhan.

Nevas.description: A villager who agrees with others to bring Baraju back home.

Chand.description: A villager who supports the idea of bringing Baraju back.

Hagboja.description: A family member, likely a child, who clings to Baraju as the family departs.

Dam.description: Baraju's young son, who is closely attached to his father.

Gauranga Sethi.description: Baraju Pradhan's elder cousin from Harpura, known for seeking Baraju's help and maintaining family ties.

Gau.description: A nickname for Gauranga Sethi, who interacts with Baraju about family matters.

Ramku.description: A household member who leaves raw rice for Chhakadi, indicating care for daily needs.

Bukula.description: A villager mentioned in Chhakadi's agitated thoughts about property and conduct.

Shisa.description: Another villager referenced in the context of property and social standing.

Bandhua.description: A villager mentioned alongside others in Chhakadi's reflections.

Jaga.description: A villager who informs others about Baraju's whereabouts.

Swara.description: A child who is usually seen reading the Bhagavata at the threshold, symbolizing the household's former liveliness.

Bha.description: A character who becomes emotional about the loss of family and property, possibly another name for Chhakadi.

Sadhuama.description: An old woman of the house, frail and reflective, who mourns the decline of the family and property.

dandak.description: A rural Odia term for a raised village path or embankment, often a gathering place for villagers.

Gopalpuri.description: Refers to tales or customs associated with the village of Gopalpur, indicating local folklore or gossip.

Brahma, Vishnu, Maheshwara.description: The Hindu trinity of gods representing creation (Brahma), preservation (Vishnu), and destruction (Maheshwara/Shiva).

Nakara.description: A person or household in the village, referenced as a place where Baraju could go for food.

Bhamara.description: A person or household in the village, mentioned as a place Gauranga visits.

Nagpur.description: A town or city, possibly referring to a nearby urban center or market town.

Bharat.description: Refers to India, used here to evoke the continuity of village life despite changes.

Kurua.description: A household or family in the village, referenced in conversation.

Damaku.description: A diminutive or affectionate form of Dam, Baraju's son.

Maipa.description: A woman in the village, possibly a relative, who cares for Damaku.

Kodka.description: A villager addressed in conversation, possibly a friend or neighbor.

Dhadha.description: A respectful or affectionate term for an elder or senior male in the village.

Basindhu Harapur.description: A family or household in the village of Harapur, associated with Gauranga Sen.

kapuri bird.description: A local bird species, possibly the Asian koel or another bird known for its distinctive call.

damara crow.description: A type of crow common in rural Odisha, known for its loud cawing.

Bharasugaon.description: A place or household name, possibly referring to the ancestral home or village.

Bakhei.description: A term indicating a price or edition, here referring to the cost of the book ('Ten Annas Each').

Manchara Manisha.description: The title of the novel, meaning 'The Simple Man' or 'Man of the Soil' in Odia.

hasboard.description: A household item, possibly a wooden board or chest used for storage.

lagapara.description: A rural household item, possibly a rope or strap used for tying bundles or livestock.

chhakada.description: A village lane or crossroads, also used as a nickname for a character.

ghada-kuncha.description: Earthen pots and cleaning brushes, common household items in rural Odisha.

betel leaf.description: A leaf from the betel plant, commonly chewed with areca nut in India.

barapipal.description: A large sacred fig tree, often a central landmark in villages.
